stem: What are the units of the coefficient of friction $\mu$?

options.rationale: Correct: μ is the ratio of two forces, F and R, so the units cancel.
μ multiplies a force (R) to give a force (F), so it cannot itself be in newtons.
This is the unit of g, the gravitational field strength.
This is the unit of acceleration.

explanation: $\mu = \frac{F}{R}$ in limiting equilibrium: newtons divided by newtons, so $\mu$ is a pure number.

stem: The frictional force on a particle resting on a rough surface is always equal to $\mu R$.
explanation: False. $F \leq \mu R$. Friction equals $\mu R$ only in limiting equilibrium or when the particle slides; otherwise it is just large enough to prevent motion.

stem: A 12 kg box rests on a rough horizontal floor. The coefficient of friction is 0.35. Take g = 9.8 m/s². Find the greatest frictional force the floor can exert, correct to 3 significant figures.
explanation: $R = 12 \times 9.8 = 117.6$ N, so $F_{\max} = \mu R = 0.35 \times 117.6 = 41.2$ N. Multiplying by the mass (4.2) forgets that $R$ is a force.
workedSolution: 1. $R = 12 \times 9.8 = 117.6$ N, so $F_{\max} = \mu R = 0.35 \times 117.6 = 41.2$ N. Multiplying by the mass (4.2) forgets that $R$ is a force.

stem: An 8 kg block on a rough horizontal surface is on the point of moving when it is pushed horizontally with a force of 23.52 N. Take g = 9.8 m/s². Find the coefficient of friction.
explanation: Limiting equilibrium: $F = \mu R$ with $F = 23.52$ N and $R = 78.4$ N, so $\mu = \frac{23.52}{78.4} = 0.3$.
workedSolution: 1. Limiting equilibrium: $F = \mu R$ with $F = 23.52$ N and $R = 78.4$ N, so $\mu = \frac{23.52}{78.4} = 0.3$.

stem: A 10 kg box rests on a rough horizontal floor with coefficient of friction 0.5. Take g = 9.8 m/s². Thandeka pushes it horizontally with a force of 30 N and it does not move. What is the frictional force on the box?

options.rationale: This is the maximum friction μR; the box needs less than this.
This is the difference 49 − 30; friction does not subtract the push from its maximum.
Correct: the box is at rest, so friction exactly balances the 30 N push.
With a push acting and no motion, friction must act to balance it.

explanation: Maximum friction = 0.5 × 98 = 49 N. The push of 30 N is less than this, so the box stays still and friction is just 30 N.

stem: A block rests on a rough inclined plane with no forces acting on it other than its weight and the contact force. In which direction does the friction on the block act?

options.rationale: Friction opposes the tendency to slide down, so it cannot act down the slope here.
Correct: without friction the block would slide down, so friction acts up the plane.
That is the direction of the normal reaction, not friction.
Friction acts along the surface, not vertically.

explanation: Friction opposes the motion that would happen without it. Here the block would slide down the plane, so friction acts up the plane.

stem: The coefficient of friction between a tin of paint and a wooden plank is 0.7. The plank is slowly tilted. Find the angle to the horizontal at which the tin is about to slide, correct to 1 decimal place.
explanation: In limiting equilibrium on a slope with no other forces, $\mu = \tan\alpha$: $\alpha = \tan^{-1} 0.7 = 35.0^\circ$. Using $\sin^{-1}$ gives $44.4^\circ$.
workedSolution: 1. In limiting equilibrium on a slope with no other forces, $\mu = \tan\alpha$: $\alpha = \tan^{-1} 0.7 = 35.0^\circ$. Using $\sin^{-1}$ gives $44.4^\circ$.

stem: A brick rests on a rough plank inclined at 28° to the horizontal and is just about to slip down it. No other forces act. Find the coefficient of friction, correct to 3 significant figures.
hints: Resolve along and perpendicular to the plank, then use F = μR.

stem: A particle rests on a rough slope of angle $\alpha$. A force $P$ acts up the line of greatest slope, and $P$ is greater than $mg\sin\alpha$. The particle does not move. In which direction does friction act?

options.rationale: Friction acts up the slope only when the particle tends to slide down, i.e. P < mg sin α.
Friction always acts along the surface.
Friction is zero only when P exactly equals mg sin α.
Correct: P alone would push the particle up the slope, so friction opposes that.

explanation: Without friction the net force along the plane would be $P - mg\sin\alpha > 0$, up the slope, so friction acts down the slope with size $P - mg\sin\alpha$ (provided this is at most $\mu R$).
hints: Which way would the particle move if the slope were smooth?

stem: A heavy trunk on a rough floor can be moved either by pushing horizontally or by pulling with a rope angled upwards. Why can the angled pull start it moving with a smaller force?

options.content: Pulling always needs less force than pushing
options.rationale: A horizontal pull and push of equal size have the same effect.

options.content: The angled pull increases the normal reaction
options.rationale: An upward component reduces the reaction; a downward push would increase it.

options.content: The upward part of the pull reduces R, so μR falls
options.rationale: Correct: R = mg − P sin θ, so the maximum friction is smaller.

options.content: The angled pull removes friction entirely
options.rationale: Friction is reduced, not removed, unless the trunk is lifted off the floor.

explanation: Vertically $R = mg - P\sin\theta$. A smaller $R$ means a smaller limiting friction $\mu R$, which can outweigh the loss of $P(1 - \cos\theta)$ in the horizontal component.

stem: A 15 kg sledge loaded with firewood rests on rough level ground, coefficient of friction 0.3. Farai pulls it with a rope at 20° above the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m/s². Find the tension in the rope when the sledge is on the point of moving, correct to 3 significant figures.
explanation: Vertically: $R = 147 - P\sin 20^\circ$. Horizontally: $P\cos 20^\circ = 0.3(147 - P\sin 20^\circ)$. So $P = \frac{44.1}{\cos 20^\circ + 0.3\sin 20^\circ} = 42.3$ N. Taking $R = 147$ N gives 46.9 N.
workedSolution:
1. Resolve vertically: $R = 147 - P\sin 20^\circ$.
2. Limiting friction: $F = 0.3R$.
3. Resolve horizontally: $P\cos 20^\circ = 0.3(147 - P\sin 20^\circ)$.
4. $P(0.9397 + 0.1026) = 44.1$, so $P = 42.3$ N.
hints: The rope lifts the sledge a little: R is not 147 N.
On the point of moving: F = μR.

stem: A 3 kg block rests on a rough plane inclined at 22° to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction is 0.5. Take g = 9.8 m/s². Find the frictional force on the block, correct to 3 significant figures.
explanation: Friction needed: $29.4\sin 22^\circ = 11.0$ N. Maximum: $0.5 \times 29.4\cos 22^\circ = 13.6$ N. As $11.0 < 13.6$ the block stays at rest and friction is 11.0 N, not $\mu R$.
workedSolution: 1. Friction needed: $29.4\sin 22^\circ = 11.0$ N. Maximum: $0.5 \times 29.4\cos 22^\circ = 13.6$ N. As $11.0 < 13.6$ the block stays at rest and friction is 11.0 N, not $\mu R$.
hints: Is the block in limiting equilibrium? Compare the friction needed with μR.

stem: A 6 kg parcel is on a rough ramp inclined at 40° to the horizontal, coefficient of friction 0.2. A force P N acts on it up the line of greatest slope. Take g = 9.8 m/s². Find the least value of P that prevents the parcel from sliding down, correct to 3 significant figures.
explanation: About to slide down, so friction acts up the ramp: $P + 0.2R = 58.8\sin 40^\circ$ with $R = 58.8\cos 40^\circ = 45.04$. $P = 37.80 - 9.01 = 28.8$ N. Friction in the wrong direction gives 46.8 N.
workedSolution:
1. $R = 58.8\cos 40^\circ = 45.04$ N, so $\mu R = 9.01$ N.
2. About to slide down: friction up the ramp.
3. $P = 58.8\sin 40^\circ - 9.01 = 37.80 - 9.01 = 28.8$ N.
hints: About to slide down: which way does friction act?

stem: The 6 kg parcel is on the same rough ramp (40°, coefficient of friction 0.2), with P acting up the line of greatest slope and g = 9.8 m/s². Find the value of P for which the parcel is about to move up the ramp, correct to 3 significant figures.
explanation: About to move up, so friction acts down the ramp: $P = 58.8\sin 40^\circ + 0.2(58.8\cos 40^\circ) = 37.80 + 9.01 = 46.8$ N.
workedSolution: 1. About to move up, so friction acts down the ramp: $P = 58.8\sin 40^\circ + 0.2(58.8\cos 40^\circ) = 37.80 + 9.01 = 46.8$ N.
hints: About to move up: friction now acts down the ramp.

stem: Match each description with the condition it gives.

left.content: At rest, not on the point of moving
About to slip on a slope with no other forces

explanation: Friction can take any value up to $\mu R$; it reaches $\mu R$ only when motion is about to start (or is happening). A smooth surface has no friction at all.

stem: A particle rests on a rough plane inclined at angle $\alpha$ to the horizontal, acted on only by its weight and the contact force, and is on the point of slipping. Show that the coefficient of friction is $\mu = \tan\alpha$.

points.description: M1 resolves perpendicular to the plane: $R = mg\cos\alpha$.
M1 resolves along the plane: $F = mg\sin\alpha$, with $F = \mu R$ (limiting).

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
$$
R = mg\cos\alpha
$$

$$
F = mg\sin\alpha
$$

Limiting equilibrium, so $F = \mu R$:

$$
mg\sin\alpha = \mu\,mg\cos\alpha \quad\Rightarrow\quad \mu = \frac{\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha} = \tan\alpha
$$

explanation: The mass cancels, so the angle of slipping depends only on the surfaces.
hints: Resolve along and perpendicular to the plane.

stem: A 25 kg box rests on a rough horizontal floor in a Mutare warehouse; the coefficient of friction is 0.45. Sipho pushes it with a force of 150 N directed downwards at 20° below the horizontal. Take g = 9.8 m/s².

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Find the normal reaction, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.explanation: Vertically: $R = 245 + 150\sin 20^\circ = 296$ N. The push has a downward component, so $R > mg$.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Vertically: $R = 245 + 150\sin 20^\circ = 296$ N. The push has a downward component, so $R > mg$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Find the greatest possible friction, correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Determine whether the box moves. Show your reasoning.

points.description: Horizontal component of the push $150\cos 20^\circ = 141$ N.
$141 > 133$, so friction cannot balance it and the box moves.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The horizontal component is $150\cos 20^\circ = 141.0$ N, greater than the maximum friction of 133.3 N, so the box starts to move.

parts.explanation: Compare the horizontal force with μR.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Find the least push at 20° below the horizontal that would just move the box, correct to 3 significant figures.

explanation: A downward push increases R and so increases the limiting friction; resolve vertically for R before using F = μR.
hints: Vertically: R balances the weight and the downward part of the push.
Limiting: horizontal part of P = μR.

stem: A 4 kg particle rests on a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal; the coefficient of friction is 0.25. A horizontal force of P N acts on the particle, in the vertical plane containing a line of greatest slope, pushing towards the plane. Take g = 9.8 m/s².

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Show that the normal reaction is $R = 39.2\cos 30^\circ + P\sin 30^\circ$.

points.description: M1 resolves perpendicular to the plane, including the component $P\sin 30^\circ$ of the horizontal force.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Perpendicular to the plane the weight has component $39.2\cos 30^\circ$ into the plane and the horizontal force has component $P\sin 30^\circ$ into the plane, so

$$
R = 39.2\cos 30^\circ + P\sin 30^\circ
$$

parts.explanation: The horizontal force makes angle 30° with the plane, so its component perpendicular to the plane is P sin 30°.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Find the least value of P that prevents the particle sliding down the plane, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.explanation: Friction up the plane: $P\cos 30^\circ + 0.25R = 39.2\sin 30^\circ$, giving $P(\cos 30^\circ + 0.125) = 39.2(0.5 - 0.2165)$, so $P = 11.2$ N.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Friction up the plane: $P\cos 30^\circ + 0.25R = 39.2\sin 30^\circ$, giving $P(\cos 30^\circ + 0.125) = 39.2(0.5 - 0.2165)$, so $P = 11.2$ N.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Find the value of P for which the particle is about to move up the plane, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.explanation: Friction down the plane: $P\cos 30^\circ = 39.2\sin 30^\circ + 0.25R$, giving $P(\cos 30^\circ - 0.125) = 39.2(0.5 + 0.2165)$, so $P = 37.9$ N.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Friction down the plane: $P\cos 30^\circ = 39.2\sin 30^\circ + 0.25R$, giving $P(\cos 30^\circ - 0.125) = 39.2(0.5 + 0.2165)$, so $P = 37.9$ N.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: State the range of values of P for which the particle remains at rest.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The particle stays at rest for $11.2 \leq P \leq 37.9$.

parts.explanation: Between the two limiting cases friction can adjust to keep the particle still.

explanation: The horizontal force has components along and into the plane, so it changes R. Use F = μR in each limiting case with friction opposing the motion that is about to happen.
hints: About to slide down: friction acts up the plane.
About to move up: friction acts down the plane.
